pages.label: Article: Why we keep doing what we regret
pages.html:
Habits · 8 min read

Why we keep doing what we regret

By the Mind Notes teamReviewed by a registered psychologist (replace)

You promised yourself you wouldn't. And yet, there you are, scrolling at midnight, again. It is easy to read this as a flaw in character. Psychology offers a gentler and more useful reading.

Habits are not decisions, they are shortcuts. The brain stores a cue, a routine and a reward, and then runs them with very little attention. Regret arrives afterwards, when attention has caught up.

Willpower is a poor plan. A better one is to change the cue.

Cue, routine, reward

Look at the cue first: the time, place, feeling or person that usually comes before the habit. Change one small thing about it, and the routine often loosens without a fight.

Make the better thing easy

Put the book on the pillow. Move the phone across the room. These are not tricks; they are how attention actually works.

This article is educational and not a substitute for professional advice. If a habit is harming you or others, please speak to a qualified professional.

pages.label: Stress check-in
pages.html:
Home/Stress check-in

A gentle check-in

Six statements about the last two weeks. About two minutes. Nothing is stored.

1. I've felt on edge or unable to relax.

2. I've had trouble switching my thoughts off at night.

3. I've felt I had too much to do and too little time.

4. I've snapped at people or felt irritable.

5. I've found it hard to enjoy things I normally like.

6. I've felt overwhelmed by small decisions.

Getting support

Reading is not treatment. Here is where to go when you need more.

If you are in immediate danger or thinking about harming yourself, contact your local emergency number now, or go to the nearest emergency department.

Talking to someone

A family doctor or general practitioner is a good first step. They can talk with you, check for physical causes and refer you to a counsellor, psychologist or psychiatrist.
